relevance_reason: The paper reports six patients from four families who carry biallelic NRROS variants and have infantile-onset seizures, neurodegeneration and intracranial calcification. This defines the SENEBAC phenotype.

findings.statement: Dong et al. (2020) reported 6 individuals from 4 families with a neurodegenerative disease. All had refractory epilepsy, developmental regression, and reduced white matter volume with delayed myelination. Development was normal or mildly delayed at first. Seizures began within the first year of life and were followed by developmental regression. Intracranial calcification was detected in 3 of the individuals.
quotes: We report six individuals from four families with bi-allelic variants in NRROS. All affected individuals had neurodegenerative disease with refractory epilepsy, developmental regression, and reduced white matter volume with delayed myelination.

The clinical course in affected individuals began with normal development or mild developmental delay, and the onset of seizures occurred within the first year of life, followed by developmental regression.
Intracranial calcification was detected in three individuals.

findings.statement: Dong et al. (2020) identified biallelic variants in the NRROS gene in 6 affected individuals from 4 families. The disease-causing variants affected 2 significant functional domains of NRROS. They produced aberrant proteins with an impaired ability to anchor latent TGF-beta-1 on the cell surface. The abstract does not name the individual variants.
quotes: We report six individuals from four families with bi-allelic variants in NRROS.

The disease-causing NRROS variants involve two significant functional NRROS domains. These variants result in aberrant NRROS proteins with impaired ability to anchor latent TGF-β1 on the cell surface.

findings.statement: Dong et al. (2020) expressed NRROS in HEK293T cells. Confocal microscopy showed that both wildtype and mutant NRROS colocalized with latent TGF-beta-1 inside the cell. Flow cytometry showed that the mutant proteins, unlike wildtype NRROS, failed to anchor latent TGF-beta-1 at the cell surface. Wildtype NRROS rescued this defect in the mutants.
quotes: Using confocal microscopy in HEK293T cells, we demonstrate that wild-type and mutant NRROS proteins co-localize with latent TGF-β1 intracellularly.
However, using flow cytometry, we show that our mutant NRROS proteins fail to anchor latent TGF-β1 at the cell surface in comparison to wild-type NRROS.
Moreover, wild-type NRROS rescues the defect of our disease-associated mutants in presenting latent TGF-β1 to the cell surface.

findings.statement: Dong et al. (2020) concluded that loss of NRROS function causes a severe childhood-onset neurodegenerative condition. They suggested that its features point to a disordered response to inflammation. The patients' features were consistent with those of the Nrros knockout mouse and overlapped with the human condition associated with TGF-beta-1 deficiency.
quotes: Taken together, our findings suggest that loss of NRROS function causes a severe childhood-onset neurodegenerative condition with features suggestive of a disordered response to inflammation.

The phenotypic features in affected individuals are consistent with those observed in the Nrros knockout mouse, and they overlap with those seen in the human condition associated with TGF-β1 deficiency.

relevance_reason: The paper reports the patients and the biallelic NRROS truncating variants that define this early-onset lethal microgliopathy with seizures, neurodegeneration and brain calcifications.

findings.statement: Smith et al. (2020) described 3 children from 2 families with a stereotyped phenotype: 2 sisters (P1 and P2) born to nonconsanguineous parents of Maori descent (family F1442), and a boy (P3) born to first-cousin South Asian parents (family F2382). Pregnancy, delivery and early development were normal. In the second year of life, the children developed refractory seizures and neurodegeneration, and they died between 27 and 36 months of age. Metabolic testing, including tests for mitochondrial dysfunction, did not find a cause.
quotes: Patients 1 (P1) and P2, both females, were the first and third children of non-consanguineous parents of Maori descent (family F1442), whilst P3 (family F2382), a male, was the first child of first cousin south Asian parents
However, in the second year of life, they experienced the onset of refractory seizures and neurodegeneration, leading to death between the ages of 27 and 36 months.
Metabolic testing, including for mitochondrial dysfunction, was non-contributory.

findings.statement: Smith et al. (2020) reported that early neuroimaging in the 3 patients showed fine calcification at the depths of the cerebral gyri, with spot and linear calcification in the deep and subcortical white matter, and normal white matter signal. As the disease progressed, repeat imaging showed more calcification, rapidly progressive severe generalized cortical and subcortical atrophy with ventricular dilatation, and diffuse signal changes in the cerebral and cerebellar white matter.
quotes: Neuroimaging initially demonstrated fine calcification at the depths of the cerebral gyri, with normal white matter (Fig. 1).
As disease progressed, repeat imaging revealed increased calcification, severe generalized atrophy with ventricular dilatation, and diffuse signal changes in cerebral and cerebellar white matter.
demonstrate widespread spot and linear calcification in the deep and sub-cortical white matter

findings.statement: Smith et al. (2020) reported that the postmortem examination of P3 found abnormalities only in the central nervous system. Findings included cerebral atrophy, focal calcification in the neuropil, and widespread neuronal loss with reactive gliosis. The most striking finding was an accumulation of foamy macrophages, mainly around blood vessels, throughout the cerebral and cerebellar white matter. These cells were positive for CD68, MHC class II and p22phox and negative for CD163, Iba1, NRROS, CD3, P2Y12 and TMEM119. Myelin basic protein was reduced, the U fibers were preserved, and there were occasional axonal spheroids. Parenchymal microglia were markedly abnormal, with loss of P2Y12 staining and weak TMEM119 staining.
quotes: The most striking pathological finding was the accumulation of foamy macrophages, predominantly in a perivascular distribution, throughout the white matter, extending from frontal to occipital white matter
There was widespread neuronal loss with reactive gliosis throughout the grey matter
There was reduced myelin basic protein (MBP) expression in the white matter (Fig. 2g) compared to age-matched controls, although there was preservation of U fibers.

phenotypes.text: perivascular foamy macrophages in white matter

phenotypes.hpo_label: Neuronal loss in central nervous system

findings.statement: Smith et al. (2020) used exome sequencing to identify a homozygous nonsense variant in NRROS, c.1777C>T (p.Gln593Ter), in the 2 affected sisters of Maori descent from family F1442. The variant is predicted to truncate the protein and had not been recorded before. No patient cells were available for functional studies.
quotes: Exome sequencing identified homozygous NRROS variants in the affected children from both families: a c.1777C > T/p.(Gln593*) and a c.1257del/p.(Gly420AlafsTer14) in F1442 and F2382, respectively.
both of these variants are predicted to result in a truncated protein, and both are very rare, with the p.(Gln593*) not previously recorded

findings.statement: Smith et al. (2020) used exome sequencing to identify a homozygous 1-bp deletion in NRROS, c.1257del (p.Gly420AlafsTer14), in a boy born to consanguineous South Asian parents (family F2382). The frameshift is predicted to truncate the protein and was present on only 1 of 251,438 alleles in gnomAD.
quotes: Exome sequencing identified homozygous NRROS variants in the affected children from both families: a c.1777C > T/p.(Gln593*) and a c.1257del/p.(Gly420AlafsTer14) in F1442 and F2382, respectively.
the p.(Gly420AlafsTer14) reported on only 1 of 251,438 alleles on gnomAD

findings.statement: Smith et al. (2020) analyzed published transcriptomic datasets. In human brain, NRROS was expressed more than 50-fold higher in microglia than in whole brain, which the authors took to mean that microglia are the main cell type expressing NRROS in brain tissue. In mouse brain, Nrros was similarly enriched in microglia and was expressed even more highly in central nervous system perivascular macrophages.
quotes: The expression of NRROS was enriched > 50-fold in microglia compared to whole brain, indicating that microglia are the major cell type expressing NRROS in human brain parenchyma.
Comparison of parenchymal microglia with CNS perivascular macrophages (PVMs) showed significantly greater expression in the latter.

findings.statement: Smith et al. (2020) reported marked upregulation of p22phox in perivascular macrophages in P3. They suggested that without functional NRROS, p22phox may bind NOX2 more, potentially increasing superoxide formation. They concluded that NRROS is essential for the early development and/or maintenance of a homeostatic microglial population, and that loss of NRROS function causes a new human microgliopathy. They noted no sign of immune-mediated inflammation.
quotes: p22phox was markedly up-regulated in PVMs in our case, suggesting that an absence of functional NRROS may result in increased p22phox-NOX2 binding, with the potential for increased superoxide radical formation.

our findings indicate that NRROS is indispensable in controlling the early development of a homeostatic microglial population and/or its ongoing preservation in the postnatal brain, thereby suggesting a loss of NRROS function as a novel microgliopathy in humans.

findings.statement: Smith et al. (2020) noted that the patients' features resemble those of Nrros-deficient mice. These mice show progressive neurological decline starting at 2 to 3 months of age and die by 6 months. Their neuropathology includes neuronal loss, demyelination, axonal pathology, astrogliosis and foamy macrophages, all of which were seen in the patient examined. The mice also lose homeostatic microglial gene expression, including P2ry12 and Tmem119.
quotes: Nrros−/−mice exhibited progressive neurological decline, including motor defects and abnormal locomotor activity, from age 2–3 months and death by 6 months of age.
Neuropathology in these mouse models includes neuronal loss, demyelination, axonal pathology, astrogliosis, and the increased presence of foamy macrophages, all of which were seen in our case.

relevance_reason: This is a mouse model of NRROS deficiency. The mice develop neurological disease and abnormal microglia, which supports the NRROS-related human disorder. The paper describes no human patients.

findings.statement: Wong et al. (2017) found that Nrros-deficient mice developed spontaneous neurological disorders, with motor defects and death before 6 months of age. Nrros-/- mice showed astrogliosis and lacked normal CD11b-hi/CD45-lo microglia, but had no detectable demyelination or neuronal loss. Instead, the CNS was populated by myeloid cells resembling perivascular macrophages.
quotes: NRROS-deficient (Nrros-/-) mice show defects in motor functions and die before 6 months of age.
Nrros-/- mice display astrogliosis and lack normal CD11bhiCD45lo microglia, but they show no detectable demyelination or neuronal loss.
Instead, perivascular macrophage-like myeloid cells populate the Nrros-/- CNS.

phenotypes.hpo_label: Neuronal loss in central nervous system

findings.statement: Wong et al. (2017) deleted Nrros using a Cx3cr1-driven system and showed that it plays a crucial role in establishing microglia during early embryonic stages. They also found that NRROS, a transmembrane protein of the endoplasmic reticulum expressed in myeloid cells, is required for normal expression of Sall1 and other microglial genes that are important for microglial development and function.
quotes: Cx3cr1-driven deletion of Nrros shows its crucial role in microglial establishment during early embryonic stages.
NRROS is required for normal expression of Sall1 and other microglial genes that are important for microglial development and function.
